passage: In the hill village, Pema had packed her school bag the night before, with the copybooks in the order of the timetable. "Careful, it's hot." Pema carried her cup with both hands to the step and blew on it. She looked back at the room, and wondered how Ama did all of this every day.

passage: Saturday morning in Prague, ten-year-old Jana was making her own sandwich for the school trip. Her father Javier stood by the counter with a cup of coffee. She buttered the bread, laid on cheese, and sliced a cucumber with the small knife, slowly, the way he had shown her, fingers curled. It took ten minutes, and she left a trail of crumbs. Then she wrapped it, put it in her bag with a water bottle and a jumper, and zipped the bag. She glanced at the pile of dishes she had used. "Papa, is this how much work you do every day?" Javier laughed. "And that was only one sandwich."

passage: In their flat in Oslo, Zeynep, nine, had a new job each evening, set by her father Lars: pack her own school bag for the next day. On the first night, she forgot her swimming kit, and on Tuesday she had to sit by the pool and watch. On Wednesday, she made a checklist with pictures: books, lunch box, swim bag, reading folder. Lars also taught her to make her bed each morning, pulling the duvet straight. It was never perfectly flat, but he left it. On Saturday, she made her own cheese sandwich while he watched, cutting it carefully with a butter knife. "It's a lot of work, being a house," she said, chewing.

qa.q: Why was Lars right to leave the duvet imperfect?

qa.q: How might Lars feel when Zeynep says it's a lot of work being a house?

passage: At the residential school in the hills, new students in Class 4 had to learn three things in the first week: pack their own bag each night, make their bed before assembly and make tea in the hostel kitchen under the warden's eye. Jaya, nine, had never done any of them at home. On Monday her bed looked like a mountain range. On Tuesday she forgot her geometry box. The warden, Yogesh sir, showed her how to tuck the sheet corners and pinned a list inside her cupboard. On Friday, she made tea for the dorm, slowly, while he stood beside the stove. It was too sweet, but everyone drank it. Jaya wrote home: "Amma, how do you do all this every day?"

qa.q: What did Jaya forget on Tuesday?
qa.a: She forgot her geometry box.

qa.q: How might Jaya have felt making tea for the dorm on Friday?
qa.a: She probably felt nervous but proud, especially when everyone drank the tea even though it was too sweet.

qa.a: He showed her how to tuck the sheet corners, pinned a list in her cupboard and stood beside her at the stove.

qa.q: How might Jaya's mother feel reading her letter?
qa.a: Her mother might feel touched and amused that Jaya now notices how much work home duties take.

passage: "Sabina, you grumble about making your bed? Sit, let your Dada Lalit tell you. When I was nine, my Ma went to help at my Mama's house for a month, and Dadi said, 'From tomorrow, you do your own mornings.' I had to fold my razai, pack my cloth bag with slate and books, and make tea for the two of us on the stove, with Dadi sitting right there on her stool, watching. The first day I forgot my slate and burnt the milk. Dadi didn't take the pan. She only said, 'Lower the flame, Lalit.' By the second week I could do it all before the school bell. And when Ma came back, I noticed something: how much she did every morning that I had never once seen."

qa.q: What happened on young Lalit's first day of doing his own mornings?
qa.a: He forgot his slate and burnt the milk.

qa.q: How might young Lalit have felt on that first morning?
qa.a: He was probably flustered and embarrassed, with a forgotten slate and burnt milk while Dadi watched.

qa.q: What choice of Dadi's was the turning point for Lalit?
qa.a: Dadi didn't take the pan from him; she only told him to lower the flame, so he kept doing it himself until he could manage alone.

qa.q: How might Ma have felt when she came back after the month?
qa.a: Ma was likely surprised and pleased to find him managing his own mornings, and maybe touched that he now noticed her work.

grounding: Shows a child who learns under supervision to fold bedding, pack a bag and make tea, and comes to see how much housework goes on at home.
